opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's more stable than people sometimes give it credit for, but with an important caveat about *which level* you're looking at.

If you zoom out, the transformer has been the dominant architecture since 2017. That's a long time in this field. And even the alternatives people get excited about, like state space models, linear attention variants, and hybrids, all still boil down to roughly the same set of primitives. You're doing a lot of matrix multiplies, some kind of sequence mixing, normalization, elementwise nonlinearities. So if you're a chip designer and your bet is "most of the FLOPs are going to be in big dense matmuls, and memory bandwidth is going to matter enormously," that bet has been right for close to a decade, and I'd expect it to stay right for a while.

Where it gets less stable is the details. The ratio of compute to memory movement shifts depending on whether you're doing training or inference, how long your contexts are, whether you're running mixture-of-experts, what precision you're using. We went from FP32 to BF16 to FP8, and now people are pushing toward even lower precision. Attention at very long context behaves very differently from attention at short context. Inference workloads, especially decoding, are often memory-bound rather than compute-bound, which is a very different design target than training. So if you overfit your chip to one specific shape of workload, you might get burned.

I'd also point out that it's a two-way street. Architectures get designed around hardware too. A lot of the reason transformers won is that they map really well to GPUs. They're parallelizable and matmul-heavy. When we worked on things like FlashAttention, the whole point was to respect the memory hierarchy of the hardware. And with newer architectures, a big part of the work is making sure they're hardware-efficient, because an idea that's theoretically elegant but can't use tensor cores just isn't going to get adopted. So there's a kind of co-evolution, and that actually creates stability. Hardware rewards certain architectures, those architectures win, and that justifies building more of that hardware.

So my advice to someone designing chips would be: bet on the primitives, not the specific model. Make matmuls fast, make memory bandwidth and capacity really good, support low precision well, and keep enough programmability that when the next attention variant or the next sparsity pattern shows up, people can actually write efficient kernels for it. The chips that get into trouble are the ones that hard-code too many assumptions about one particular model.

r001.rationale: It describes transformers as stable at a high level while saying the details and workload patterns continue to change, including mixture-of-experts and attention variants.

r002.rationale: It mentions mixture-of-experts but does not say that these models can have more parameters while requiring less computation than dense models.

r003.rationale: It does not identify mixture-of-experts sparsity as a challenge for chips designed around uniform, dense computation.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because the timelines are so mismatched. Designing a chip takes two to three years from architecture decision to silicon in a datacenter. Model architectures, at least on the surface, seem to change every six months. So if you bet on the exact architecture of today, you'll probably be wrong by the time the chip ships.

But I'd actually argue the picture is more stable than it looks. If you zoom out, the transformer has been the dominant architecture since 2017, and the core computational primitives haven't changed that much. It's still mostly matrix multiplication, plus some kind of attention or token-mixing operation, plus elementwise and normalization layers. The matmul part is extremely stable. Every architecture I can imagine being competitive in the next few years is going to be dominated by matmuls, whether that's a dense transformer, a mixture of experts, or a state-space model. So the tensor cores, the systolic arrays, those are a safe bet.

Where it gets interesting is the non-matmul parts, and the memory system. A lot of what we did with FlashAttention was really about the fact that the hardware had tons of compute but relatively little memory bandwidth, and attention as naively implemented was bandwidth-bound. So the algorithm adapted to the hardware. That's a lesson in itself: the co-design goes both ways. If chip designers give us more SRAM, or a different memory hierarchy, or better support for things like softmax or exponentials, the algorithms will move to exploit that. Hardware shapes which architectures win, not just the other way around. Transformers partly won because they map so well onto GPUs.

So my view is that you shouldn't design for a specific architecture. You should design for the workload characteristics that are likely to persist: large matmuls at lower and lower precision, some sequence-mixing operation that needs to be memory-efficient, and increasingly, inference with long contexts where the KV cache or the state is the bottleneck. Mixture of experts adds a need for fast routing and memory capacity. Those trends feel robust to me even if the exact layer definitions change.

The risk is over-specializing. If someone built a chip that hard-wired a particular attention variant, or assumed a specific sequence length or head dimension, that chip could look very outdated quickly. The chips that have aged well are the ones that kept a lot of programmability around a very fast matmul engine. I'd rather have a slightly less efficient chip that I can write new kernels for than a perfectly efficient one for an architecture nobody uses anymore.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the transformer’s continued dominance and stable core computations with architectures that appear to change frequently and layer definitions that may change.

r002.rationale: It mentions mixture-of-experts but does not say that MoE models can have more parameters while requiring less computation than dense models.

r003.rationale: It notes MoE’s need for fast routing and memory capacity, but does not identify MoE sparsity as a mismatch for chips built around uniform, dense computation.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what level you look at. If you’re betting on the exact architecture staying the same—the particular attention mechanism or how the layers are arranged—that seems risky. There’s still a lot of experimentation happening.

But if you go down a level, the underlying operations are much more stable. Matrix multiplication has been central for a long time, and I would expect it to remain central even if the architecture changes. Moving data efficiently between memory and compute is also going to matter regardless of which model wins.

So I’d be more comfortable designing around those primitives while keeping flexibility in how you compose them. The challenge is that specialization gives you efficiency, but a chip takes a long time to design. You want to specialize enough to get a meaningful advantage without making a bet that only works for today’s model.

r001.rationale: It says specific attention mechanisms and layer arrangements may change, but does not communicate apparent stability at the transformer level.

r002.rationale: It does not mention mixture-of-experts models, parameter counts, or their computation needs.

r003.rationale: It does not identify mixture-of-experts sparsity or explain its challenge for chips built around dense computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what level you look at. At the level of the whole architecture, I wouldn’t bet that the Transformer we use today is exactly what we’ll use five years from now. But if you look at the underlying operations, there’s a lot more stability. Matrix multiplication has been central for a long time, and I think that’s a much safer thing to design around.

The other part is data movement. Whatever the architecture is, moving data between memory and the compute units is expensive. So having fast matrix multiplication, enough memory bandwidth, and flexibility in how you move data seems like a pretty robust investment.

Where I’d be more cautious is building hardware that assumes a very particular form of attention, or a particular sequence length. Algorithms change partly in response to the hardware we have. You want enough flexibility to take advantage of those changes.
